title: 181 Level of cotton gin byproduct in growing diets for stocker cattle
content:
Abstract
Cotton gin byproduct (also known as gin trash), is an underutilized byproduct feed for beef cattle that is widely available across the southern USA. Cotton gin byproduct (CGB) has been fed in a wide variety of diets to beef cattle, especially dry brood cows. This study was conducted to determine how CGB level in the diet influenced beef steer performance during the growing phase and subsequent finishing performance when fed a typical feedlot ration. Seventy five Angus steers (initial BW 353 ± 66 kg) were stratified by body weight into groups of 15, and then assigned to one of 5 pens representing each weight block (3 steers/pen). Each pen was randomly assigned within block to one of five diets containing 0, 10, 20, 30, and 40% CGB (dry matter basis). Corn silage, corn, soybean meal and minerals made up the remainder of the diet. Diets were balanced for crude protein, minerals, and TDN (assuming a TDN of 50% for the CGB), and were fed for 84 days. Following the growing period, steers were switched to a single finishing diet and fed for an additional 70 days prior to being transported to PA for harvest and carcass data collection. Data was analyzed using procMIXED of SASv9.4 to determine the significance of linear, quadratic, cubic, and quartic trends. The CGB contained an average of 89.1% DM, 11.6% CP, 7.7% ash and 56.6% NDF. During the growing phase, DMI increased linearly (P = 0.001) with 11.17, 11.19, 13.85, 14.84, and 13.93 kg/day; ADG increased linearly (P = 0.01) with 1.80, 1.93, 1.95, 1.97, and 2.01 kg/day; and feed efficiency (kg ADG/kg DMI) showed linear (P = 0.0127) and cubic (P = 0.0365) effects with 0.163, 0.176, 0.143, 0.136, and 0.145 for 0, 10, 20, 30, and 40% CGB, respectively. During the finishing phase DMI showed linear and quadratic effects (P < 0.05), with 12.60, 12.17, 11.00, 11.07, and 11.4 kg/d; ADG showed linear, quadratic and quartic effects (P < 0.05) with 1.48, 1.51, 1.08, 1.29, and 1.37 kg/d; and feed efficiency showed linear and quartic effects (P < 0.05) with 0.118, 0.125, 0.098, 0.117, and 0.121 for 0, 10, 20, 30 and 40 % CGB, respectively. Both marbling and quality grade increased linearly (P = 0.05; P = 0.013, respectively). Marbling scores were 6.33, 6.13, 6.37, 6.52, and 6.81, while quality grade scores were 17.8, 17.73, 18.00, 18.21, and 18.36 for 0, 10, 20, 30, and 40% CGB, respectively. This study showed that CGB is a viable byproduct feed for high producing beef calves during the growing phase. Carry over effects into the finishing period show a need for additional research to better understand impacts throughout the full lifecycle.
